sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Pub/Sub is a messaging pattern where producers publish messages to a topic without knowing subscribers, and each subscriber receives an independent copy of every message — enabling fan-out, loose coupling, and independent consumption rates per subscriber.

Pub/Sub (publish/subscribe) inverts the coupling of point-to-point queues: instead of a producer sending a message to one consumer via a queue, the producer publishes to a topic, and the broker delivers a copy of each message to every subscriber. The producer is unaware of how many subscribers exist, where they run, or how slow they are — the broker manages fan-out. This pattern is the backbone of event-driven architectures at scale: Netflix's "video viewed" event is published once and consumed independently by the recommendation service, the analytics pipeline, the billing service, and the fraud detector; Uber's "trip completed" event fans out to billing, receipts, surge pricing, and driver-rating services. Google Pub/Sub, AWS SNS, Kafka (via consumer groups), and Redis Pub/Sub are the canonical implementations. The pattern's power is decoupling: adding a new consumer (a new microservice that reacts to user sign-ups) requires no change to the producer or to existing consumers — you subscribe and start receiving.

The defining feature of pub/sub is **fan-out**: one published message becomes N copies, one per subscriber. In Kafka, this is implemented via consumer groups — each group has its own offset on the topic, so multiple groups consume the same messages independently. In Google Pub/Sub and AWS SNS, each subscription is a separate queue that the broker writes a copy of the message to; the subscriber then pulls from its own queue at its own pace. In Redis Pub/Sub (the "fire and forget" variant), the broker pushes messages to currently-connected subscribers with no durability — if a subscriber is offline, it misses the message. The two durability models split the market: **durable pub/sub** (Kafka, Google Pub/Sub, SNS+SQS) persists messages so offline subscribers catch up on reconnect, while **ephemeral pub/sub** (Redis Pub/Sub, MQTT) delivers only to currently-connected subscribers, trading durability for sub-millisecond latency. The architect's choice: durable for any subscriber whose missing a message has consequences (billing, analytics), ephemeral for real-time push where stale messages are noise (chat presence, live sports scores).

Real-world deployments illustrate the trade-offs. Google Pub/Sub is the fully-managed durable pub/sub of GCP: topics accept millions of messages/sec, subscriptions are pull-based with ack and at-least-once delivery, and message retention defaults to 7 days. Spotify uses Google Pub/Sub for its "track played" event, which fans out to royalty accounting, recommendation training, and the real-time dashboard. AWS SNS is the equivalent on AWS: a topic fans out to SQS queues (one per subscriber), Kinesis streams, Lambda functions, or HTTP endpoints; SNS+SQS is the most common pattern because it gives each subscriber its own durable queue with independent consumption. Kafka's consumer-group model is subtly different: a topic has N partitions, and within a consumer group each partition is consumed by one consumer (load-balanced); across consumer groups, each group sees all messages (fan-out). So Kafka gives you both load balancing (within a group) and pub/sub (across groups) in one primitive — which is why it has displaced most specialized pub/sub brokers at large scale.

The trade-off pub/sub forces is the cost of fan-out. One published message becomes N copies, so the broker's outbound bandwidth is N× the inbound bandwidth. For a topic with 1MB/sec ingress and 20 subscribers, the broker pushes 20MB/sec outbound — manageable. For a topic with 1GB/sec ingress and 100 subscribers (Netflix's "user activity" stream), outbound is 100GB/sec, which is why Netflix uses Kafka with selective consumer-side filtering rather than separate topics per consumer. The second trade-off is per-subscriber back-pressure: a slow subscriber's queue grows independently, and the broker must either grow its storage (Kafka's retention), drop messages (ephemeral), or apply back-pressure to the producer (which would affect all subscribers — usually undesirable). The standard answer is per-subscriber queues with bounded storage and per-subscriber monitoring: if the analytics subscriber's queue exceeds 1M messages, alert; if the billing subscriber's queue exceeds 100 messages, page, because billing latency is user-visible. The architect must classify subscribers by latency tolerance and set per-subscriber SLOs, not treat all subscribers equally.

The third trade-off is **delivery semantic and ordering**. Durable pub/sub systems offer at-least-once delivery (the subscriber may receive duplicates and must be idempotent), and per-key ordering is preserved only within a partition (Kafka) or a message-group (Google Pub/Sub with ordering keys, SNS FIFO). Cross-key ordering is impossible at scale because messages are produced in parallel. The architect's rule: design subscribers to be idempotent (keyed on `event_id`, with a dedup table or unique constraint), and design partition keys to preserve per-entity ordering (e.g., `user_id` so all events for one user are ordered). The result is a system where the producer fires one event, N subscribers react independently at their own pace, and the system scales by adding subscribers without touching producers — the cleanest decoupling in distributed systems design, and the foundation of every modern event-driven microservices architecture.

### Mermaid Diagram ```mermaid flowchart TD P[Publisher
video-viewed event] P -->|publish| T[Topic: video.viewed] T -->|copy 1| S1[Subscription: recs] T -->|copy 2| S2[Subscription: analytics] T -->|copy 3| S3[Subscription: billing] T -->|copy 4| S4[Subscription: fraud] S1 --> C1[Recommendation Svc] S2 --> C2[Analytics Svc] S3 --> C3[Billing Svc] S4 --> C4[Fraud Svc] style T fill:#ffd,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px style S1 fill:#dfd style S2 fill:#dfd style S3 fill:#dfd style S4 fill:#dfd ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` +-----------------+ publish | Topic: | publisher ------------>| video.viewed | +---+---+---+----+ | | | | fan-out (1 msg -> N copies) copy 1 ___| | | | copy 4 copy 2 _______| | |_____ copy 3 ___________| \ v v v v +----+ +----+ +----+ +----+ |recs| |anal| |bill| |frud| independent subscriptions +--+-+ +--+-+ +--+-+ +--+-+ | | | | v v v v recs.svc analytics billing fraud.svc (own pace, own ack, own retry, own DLQ) ``` ### Walkthrough 1. The publisher publishes one `video.viewed` message to the topic; the broker durably stores it (in Kafka: appended to the topic's partition log). 2. The broker fans out a copy of the message to each subscription — recommendation, analytics, billing, fraud — each with its own offset/queue, consumption rate, and ack. 3. Each subscriber processes at its own pace and acks independently; a slow subscriber (analytics) does not block a fast one (fraud), and the producer is unaffected by any subscriber's health.

quiz.explanation: A point-to-point queue delivers each message to exactly one consumer (load-balanced), while pub/sub delivers a copy of each message to every subscriber (fan-out). The two patterns solve different problems. Point-to-point is for parallelizing work: 100 order-processing workers pull from one orders queue, each order processed by one worker — total throughput is the sum of worker throughputs.

quiz.explanation: Kafka's pub/sub emerges from the consumer-group abstraction. A topic has N partitions; each partition is an append-only log. Within a single consumer group, partitions are assigned to consumers one-to-one (or one-to-many if there are fewer consumers than partitions), so the group as a whole sees each message exactly once — this is point-to-point / load balancing.

quiz.question: What is the difference between durable and ephemeral pub/sub? Give an example of each.
options: At-least-once delivery means each subscriber receives every message at least once, but may receive duplicates (typically due to redelivery after a crash or a network retry).
This is why Kafka scales to thousands of consumer groups per topic.
Sending every price change to all 1000 cache pods is wasteful: most pods do not have the affected product in their cache, so the message is a no-op.
Durable pub/sub persists messages until every subscriber has acked (or until retention expires), so a subscriber that is offline when a message is published receives it on reconnect.
quiz.explanation: Durable pub/sub persists messages until every subscriber has acked (or until retention expires), so a subscriber that is offline when a message is published receives it on reconnect. Ephemeral pub/sub delivers messages only to subscribers that are currently connected; an offline subscriber misses the message permanently.

quiz.explanation: Per-key ordering requires that all messages with the same key are delivered to the same consumer in the same order they were produced. In Kafka, this is automatic: the producer sets a partition key (e.g., user_id), the broker hashes the key to a partition, and within a partition messages are in append order. Each consumer group has one consumer per partition, so that consumer sees the user's events in order.
